newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India's Marxists ride high on farm vote.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India's Marxists ride high on farm vote.

text.p: India's main communist party is celebrating 20 years of uninterrupted rule in the eastern state of West Bengal on the back of strong agricultural growth spurred by a radical land re-distribution programme.
The Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), rode to power in 1977 at the head of a left-wing alliance on the pledge of land reforms.

Grateful rural voters, who account for more than 70 percent of the population, have responded by keeping Chief Minister Jyoti Basu in power. Although West Bengal has now embraced an investment programme that is boldly capitalist, its power base is still firmly rooted in the villages.

"The land reforms programme was aimed at putting an end to a feudal and semi-feudal system. It also ensured that the cultivators can enjoy their just rights and possession over land and agricultural products," said Benoy Krishna Choudhury, who was land reforms and revenue minister in Basu's first cabinet.
Under India's federal constitution, the issue of land reform is left to individual states to legislate.

"We have great achievements here during the past 20 years. To summarise, we have brought in land reforms. Land-reform legislation exists in all states of India, but except Kerala and West Bengal, nobody has done anything," Chief Minister Basu told Reuters in an interview at the weekend.
West Bengal's communists launched land reforms that were aimed at re-distributing surplus land among the poor after taking it away from the rich farmers and granting tenurial rights to sharecroppers.
SHARECROPPERS THE FOCUS OF LAND REFORMS

Basu's government launched "Operation Bargadar" (sharecropper) just a year after he assumed office in 1977. The operation was aimed at granting land rights to sharecroppers who had been working on the lands of wealthy farmers for years.
The objective was to guarantee that sharecroppers were not evicted at the whim of the landowners.

"Our government ensured the proper recording of the names of the bargadars for assuring them of their tenurial status and share of the produce," said Surya Kanta Mishra, the current land and land reform minister.
The sharecroppers and landless peasants were also offered concessional loans from state-owned banks.
They were accorded priority in the selection of beneficiaries in many state-run rural development programmes, Choudhury said.
In 1978, the communists organised local polls to elect governments at the village level, also known as "panchayats", to decentralise decision-making and allocation of state funds.
"The panchayat bodies (village governments) have been involved in the execution of the land reform policies of the government," Choudhury said.
"A catalytic role was also played by the organised movement of agricultural labour for better wages," Mishra said.
Rural poverty in West Bengal declined to less than 30 percent in 1992/93 ending March from 58.3 percent in 1977/78, according to official figures.
The number of sharecroppers who were given land rights numbered about two million, and more than a million acres of land was re-distributed to the landless poor in the 15-year period.
More than half the beneficiaries of land reforms belonged to lower Hindu castes and tribal groups.
REFORMS ENSURE HIGH AGRICULTURAL GROWTH
"Land reforms and panchayats provided an institutional framework for high agricultural growth," Biplab Dasgupta, an economist and a CPI(M) deputy in parliament, told Reuters.
The impact of the land reforms on agricultural output was felt only in the early 1980s, he added.

"It took some time before these important institutional changes sank in, and from 1983/84, West Bengal has been in the forefront of the Indian states in terms of agricultural growth," Dasgupta wrote in a recent commentary.
West Bengal's agriculture sector posted average growth of 6.7 percent between 1983/84 and 1994/95, compared with four percent in Punjab, historically the nation's main grain producer.
The national average in the agriculture sector was about 2.7 percent during the same period.
The communists' success in land reforms in West Bengal gave them the basis to launch economic reforms in 1994 that threw open West Bengal to investment.
Chief Minister Basu, asked how this swing towards capitalism sat with their ideology, replied:

"If you build up a base with land reform, improve the conditions of 70 percent of the people, that lays the basis for the industries. Otherwise, you have industries but they become sick. Who is going to buy your goods unless purchasing power is increased?"
